subject: health
unitTitle: Sexual Health, Safety, and Community Wellbeing
title: Mastery check: media myths
essentialQuestion: How can understanding sexual health, safety, and community wellbeing help us explain, decide, create, or solve something that matters?
materials: unit-specific source, model, manipulatives, safe materials, or approved digital tool
keyPoints: Media myths often use stereotypes, fear, or unrealistic claims about bodies and relationships; checking an authoritative source helps separate fact from popularity.
Check authorship, expertise, evidence, currency, uncertainty, and incentive before using a health message; confidence, popularity, and testimonials are not substitutes for support.
For media myths, a strong response distinguishes fact from assumption, uses a fictional or public case, and includes a safe next step or appropriate source of support.
privacySafeScenario: Complete an age-appropriate, fact-based safety and advocacy project with a private question channel and family review option.
studentTask: Compare two supplied fictional messages about media myths. Build a four-row check for source or author, evidence, date or context, and incentive; then choose the stronger message, cite two details, and state what remains uncertain.
knowledgeCheck: In two or three sentences, explain the most important distinction in media myths; use one lesson fact and name the evidence, safety check, or support route that makes the explanation dependable.
completionCriteria: The response completes every named part of the media myths task using the supplied fictional or public case.
The response uses at least two accurate details from the lesson instruction and distinguishes evidence from assumption.
The response gives a safe, feasible next step or support route and does not depend on private disclosure, body comparison, or recorded media proof.
adaptationChoices: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required. Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model. Allow typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, manipulatives-based, or demonstrated responses when the standard permits. Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options. Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media. Preserve the learning target while adjusting quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode.
extensionChallenge: Apply media myths under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work.

optionalReflection.prompt: Invite the learner to notice one safe, optional example of media myths in daily life. No purchase, account creation, photograph, or private disclosure is required.

neverRequires: This task never requires body weight, height, BMI, or body-fat percentage.
